$comment: Rules are DATA, not code (docs/05_DETECTION.md). This file ships with the
app and is updatable from the repository independently of releases.
The `anticheat` block is what feeds the hard gate in
docs/19_SAFETY_AND_ANTICHEAT.md. Updates to it are treated as security
updates: applied on the next check regardless of the user's auto-update
preference for other rules. Removing an entry is a safety change and needs
the same review as a security fix (docs/13_CI_CD.md §rules-publish).
Shape is fixed by rules/detection-rules.schema.json (JSON Schema 2020-12),
which closes docs/20_OPEN_QUESTIONS.md §S5. Constraints a schema cannot
express — duplicate ids, over-broad prefixes that shadow system DLLs, regex
compilability, case-insensitive duplicate values — stay imperative in
tools/rules-validate.ps1.

$comment: 19_SAFETY: name fragment AND not signed by a known vendor => warn-and-refuse.
trustedSigners are matched against the certificate subject's O= field, NOT CN=.
Measured 2026-08-02 on Windows 11 26300, and the two fields genuinely differ:
kernel32.dll   CN='Microsoft Windows'  O='Microsoft Corporation'
nvapi64.dll    CN='Microsoft Windows Hardware Compatibility Publisher'  O='Microsoft Corporation'
nvlddmkm.sys   CN='Microsoft Windows Hardware Compatibility Publisher'  O='Microsoft Corporation'
nvrla.exe      CN='NVIDIA Corporation'  O='NVIDIA Corporation'
steam.exe      CN='Valve Corp.'  O='Valve Corp.'
That WHQL CN is why the field matters. Every WHQL-signed binary on the
machine — including the NVIDIA display driver itself — carries it, and it
is not a vendor name. Matching on CN would make the entire driver stack
read as untrusted; paired with the 'guard'/'protect' nameFragments below,
that is a false-refusal path, not a theoretical one. O= survives WHQL
re-signing and is what the guard must compare.
UNTESTED: 'Intel Corporation' and 'Advanced Micro Devices, Inc.' are still
guesses. This machine has an RTX 5080, no AMD or Intel GPU and no iGPU
(docs/spike-notes.md §Environment), so neither string can be measured here.
Untested, not wrong — and not to be presented as measured.
